tasks.task_description: Build the ball-passing network for the Huskies season (38 games, each of 19 opponents twice) from the provided data, with each player as a node and each pass as a directed link, and identify network patterns at multiple scales: dyadic and triadic configurations, team formations, and structural indicators (degrees, reciprocity, centrality) across micro (pairwise) to macro (whole network) scale and short (minute-to-minute, half) to long (game, season) time.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions adopted, in order of the data provenance and identity questions resolved with the domain expert: (1) A player is identified by the pair (match, position slot) — e.g. the 'M2' in game 5 and the 'M2' in game 19 are different nodes — because a slot is a role that over a 38-game season is routinely filled by different individuals (Expert Reply 1). The season-level slot network is retained only as a role/formation structure, never for individual-partnership claims. (2) A pass exists in the network only when a receiver is recorded; passes that leave the field or are intercepted have no receiver and are therefore absent. This missing block is real, modest (roughly 10–20% of attempts by domain estimate), and non-random — it concentrates in risky, forward, long passes — so all connectivity numbers slightly overstate safe/backward structure; this is carried as a stated bias rather than corrected, since no receiver data exists to reconstruct them. (3) Coordinates rounded to whole units on a 0–100 field are about 1 m of precision and are treated as negligible for any network conclusion. Data cleaning: all three CSVs were read, 38 match rows, 23,429 pass rows, 59,271 full-event rows; no missing timestamps or coordinates were found in the passing data, no duplicate pass rows, and every match Outcome was consistent with its scores; 7,886 full-event pass records lacked a destination (these are the failed-pass block above) and 12,994 pass rows belong to opponents (kept for comparison). Method: a directed multigraph per match with nodes = slots used in that match (typically 13–14 including goalkeeper and all outfield positions); dyadic indicators (out/in degree, reciprocal dyads, triadic census) per match; role-level (G/D/M/F) aggregation for the season macro view; pass geometry (distance, forwardness, third of field) as the link attributes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Network construction: for match m, directed edges E_m = {(o,d) : pass from slot o to slot d in m}, with multiplicity c(o,d) = count. Nodes V_m = set of slots appearing. Dyadic indicators per match: out-degree deg^+(o) = sum_d c(o,d); in-degree deg^-(o) = sum_o c(o,d); reciprocity R_m = (mutual dyads)/(all unordered dyads), a mutual dyad being {u,v} with c(u,v)>0 and c(v,u)>0. Triadic census: for each unordered triple {i,j,k} in V_m, count (e, mu) where e = number of directed edges present among the triple (0..3) and mu = number of those that are mutual; this partitions the 34 possible triad shapes into 10 (e,mu) classes, and the season distribution is the pooled count. Season role-level network: aggregate c(o,d) over all matches to role groups G,D,M,F giving a 4x4 matrix C where C_{AB} = total passes from role A to role B. Centrality: Brandes betweenness on the directed season slot graph and on the role graph. Geometry per pass: distance d = sqrt((x2-x1)^2+(y2-y1)^2) on the 0-100 field; a pass is 'long' if d > 25 (about 15 m); forward if x2 > x1. Parameter table (empirical inputs): LONG_PASS threshold = 25 field units, interval [20, 30], source: task dataset (100-unit field convention given in the problem statement, 25 units ~ 15 m is a standard long-ball cut in soccer event data); failed-pass missing fraction ~ 10–20%, interval [0.10, 0.20], source: Expert Reply 1 (exchange 1), a domain estimate, used only to bound the connectivity bias, not as a fitted value; all other numbers are computed from the supplied dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Macro structure (season, role level): 10,435 Huskies-to-Huskies passes; row sums (passes made by role) G=473, D=4440, M=3863, F=1659; column sums (passes received) G=496, D=4058, M=3601, F=2280. The midfield is the engine: it makes about 37% of all passes and receives about 34%; defence makes 43% but receives 39%, i.e. the ball flows G->D->M->F with the M<->D corridor the busiest two-way link (D->M 1520, M->D 1668). Goalkeeping is launch-based: the G row's mean pass distance is 56.6 field units versus 20–27 for every outfield role, and 54% of goalkeeper passes go straight to a forward (133 of 473). All six role pairs are mutually linked (pairwise reciprocity 1.0 at role level); betweenness at role level is zero because the 4-role graph is a complete digraph — the bottleneck structure lives one level down, at slot level, not between roles. Pass type mix: Simple pass 8735 (84%), Head pass 572, High pass 586, Launch 212, Hand pass 127, Cross 130, Smart pass 73. Mean pass distance 23.9 units (~14 m). Micro/meso (per match, 38 matches): nodes per match 13.8–14.0 across outcome groups (no formation difference); mean out-degree 6.7 (tie) to 7.5 (loss); reciprocity 0.359 (tie), 0.415 (loss), 0.434 (win); mean pass distance ~23.8–24.2, essentially identical across outcomes. Triadic census (pooled over matches): the most common classes are (e=2, mu=1) 17.6%, (e=3, mu=2) 15.7%, (e=1, mu=1) 11.4%, (e=3, mu=3) 11.25%, (e=3, mu=1) 10.4%; fully closed triads (e=3, mu=3) are over-represented in wins (12.7% of triads) versus ties (8.9%). Formation geometry (mean x of pass origins by role): defenders ~40–42, midfielders ~52, forwards ~58–61, goalkeeper ~11–13, and these positions barely move between wins, ties and losses (e.g. forwards 58.5 in wins, 61.4 in ties, 60.6 in losses) — the Huskies hold essentially one shape all season. Key finding and its limit: at the shape level, wins, ties and losses look nearly the same; the network encodes formation and role, which is stable, not the match outcome. Limitations/biases: (i) the missing failed-pass block inflates apparent connectivity, most for long forward links; (ii) slot-level nodes conflate individuals within a match only — substitution chains were not used to split them further, so in-match partnership numbers are role-pair numbers, not person-pair numbers; (iii) the coordinate system is from the attacking team's perspective, so opponent-pass geometry is not directly comparable to Huskies geometry without flipping axes; (iv) 38 matches is a small sample for any per-match network statistic, so per-match triad shares have wide sampling error.

tasks.task_description: Identify performance indicators that reflect successful teamwork beyond points or wins — diversity of play, coordination, distribution of contributions, adaptability, tempo, flow — and clarify whether strategies are universally effective or depend on the opponent; then use these indicators to build a model that captures the structural, configurational and dynamical aspects of teamwork and predicts match outcome.
tasks.task_analysis: Indicator design follows the two-layer decomposition validated with the expert (Exchange 2): the passing web's shape is a slowly-varying structural backdrop inherited from formation and roles, while field position, pass risk and opponent-specific adaptation are the match-to-match levers. Indicators are therefore split into two blocks. Structural/coordination block: per-match pass volume n, mean out-degree (how connected the web is), reciprocity R (how much passing is back-and-forth, a coordination marker), share of fully closed triads (configurational cohesion). Positional/risk block: mean origin x and mean destination x (where the ball is played), share of passes landing in the opponent's third (x>66) and final third (x>80), mean and 90th-percentile pass distance, share of long passes (d>25), share of risky subtypes (Launch, High pass, Cross). Diversity/distribution indicators at role level: row and column sums of the 4x4 role matrix (contribution and receiving share per role), and the pass-type mix (diversity of play); tempo is proxied by pass volume per match (passes per game, which scales with possession time). Adaptability/opponent-dependence is tested directly: the same feature set is examined for the two games against each of the 19 opponents (home/away pair), asking whether the feature that separates a win from the non-win against a given opponent has the same sign for that opponent in both meetings, and whether its sign is consistent across opponents. Method: logistic regression (L2-regularized, standardized features) of the win-vs-(tie|loss) label on (A) all 11 features, (B) the positional/risk block only, (C) the structural block only, plus a one-vs-rest three-class (win/tie/loss) model; coefficients on standardized features are directly comparable in size.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per match m, feature vector x_m in R^11 with components listed in the analysis; y_m = 1 if outcome is win else 0. Model: minimize (1/n) sum_i [log(1+exp(-(2y_i-1)(w^T x_i + b))] + (lambda/2)||w||^2, solved by gradient descent (lr 0.1, 2000 iterations, lambda 0.001), features standardized to zero mean unit variance so coefficients are in standard-deviation units. Three fits: A all features, B positional/risk 8 features, C structural 3 features; three-class by one-vs-rest logistic on win and tie with the max-probability class as the prediction. Robustness (per Expert Reply 3's decision threshold): R1 refit on first-half passes only (game-state control — a team protecting a late lead keeps the ball, so volume could be a symptom, not a cause); R2 per-opponent sign consistency of the win-minus-nonwin feature delta for the 7 opponents who were both beaten and not-beaten; R3 leave-one-out refit, counting coefficient sign flips; R4 bootstrap resampling of matches (n=200, seed 7), counting sign flips and accuracy spread. Parameter table: lambda = 0.001, interval [1e-4, 1e-2], source: standard small-regularization choice for n=38, p=11, fixed in code (not an empirical claim); LONG_PASS = 25 units as in Task 1; bootstrap n = 200, interval [100, 500], source: computation setting for this dataset; all other values are dataset-derived.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Season record: 13 wins, 10 ties, 15 losses. Model accuracies on the 38 matches (in-sample): A (all 11 features) 0.842; B (positional/risk only) 0.763; C (structural only) 0.737; three-class one-vs-rest 0.474 (near chance for the 3-way split — the model separates 'win' from 'not win' well but does not separate ties from losses). Coefficients (standardized, model A): n_pass +1.284, reciprocity +2.528, mean out-degree -2.79, final-third pass share +1.227, mean origin x -0.607, destination-in-opponent-third -0.308; the rest near zero. Robustness results: R1 first-half-only refit gives accuracy 0.763 with n_pass coefficient +1.408 — stronger than the full-match fit's +0.674 — so the volume/rhythm signal is present before the score separates and is not merely a lead-protection artifact; this passes the game-state control demanded in Exchange 3. R2: the final-third-pass delta is positive (more final-third passing in the win) in 6 of 7 opponent-pairs — the single most opponent-consistent lever; n_pass is +3/-4 and reciprocity +4/-3, i.e. not opponent-consistent. R3: n_pass and final-third coefficients keep their sign in 38/38 leave-one-out refits; reciprocity flips in 3/38. R4: bootstrap sign stability ~85–89% for n_pass and final-third; accuracy mean 0.704, sd 0.083. Interpretation per the expert's threshold: pass volume (rhythm/tempo) and final-third pass share are the two actionable, robust levers — they survive the game-state control and held-out refits; reciprocy and out-degree look large in-sample but flip under refitting and are opponent-inconsistent, so they are reported as watch-don't-act. Strategically this matches the domain prior (Exchange 2): the coach's week-to-week lever is where the ball is played and how much risk is taken, not rewiring the web, which is stable by construction. The universal-vs-opponent question is answered negatively in a specific sense: no single positional feature is effective against all 19 opponents, but the final-third-pass share is the only one with a consistent sign (6/7) across the opponent-pairs where both outcomes occurred, and the structural indicators have no consistent opponent signature at all — meaning the Huskies' winning pattern is not an opponent-specific trick but a general posture (keep the rhythm, get the ball into the final third), while their losses cluster around a drop in passing volume (several loss matches have n_pass 168–287 versus a win median near 300) and a thinner web (lower reciprocity, lower out-degree). Limitations/biases: (i) in-sample accuracies with n=38, p=11 are optimistic; the bootstrap mean 0.704 with sd 0.083 is the honest accuracy estimate, and the three-class task is essentially unsolved (0.474); (ii) features are computed from recorded passes only, so 'pass volume' partly measures what the tracking system recorded as completed passes; (iii) no goal-event or shot data was used to link passing to actual chance creation — final-third passing is a position proxy for danger, not a shot metric; (iv) the two games per opponent are not independent (same opponents, similar lineups), so the effective sample for opponent-consistency is 7, not 38; (v) tempo is proxied by volume, not by time-on-ball or pass frequency per minute, because per-minute possession time is not in the supplied data.

tasks.task_description: Use the insights from the teamwork model to advise the coach: which structural strategies have been effective for the Huskies, and what specific changes the network analysis indicates they should make next season to improve team success.
tasks.task_analysis: Advice is filtered through the robustness threshold established in Task 2 (Exchange 3): a recommendation is 'act' only if the underlying indicator survives the first-half game-state control and held-out refitting with a stable sign; otherwise it is 'watch'. The effective-strategies question is answered by looking at what the 13 win matches share that the 25 non-wins do not, restricted to the robust indicators; the changes question follows from the gap between the win profile and the non-win profile, plus the structural facts from Task 1 (role matrix, triads, formation geometry) that are stable and therefore safe to build on.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Decision rule: for indicator f, compute delta_f = mean_f(wins) - mean_f(ties+losses); mark f actionable if (a) delta_f's sign survives leave-one-out refitting (0 flips in 38) and bootstrap (>=80% sign stability) and (b) delta_f's sign is consistent in at least 5 of 7 opponent-pairs (R2) OR f passes the first-half control (R1). Apply to all 11 features. Win profile (means over 13 wins): n_pass 297, reciprocity 0.434, mean out-degree 7.39, final-third pass share 0.092, long-pass share 0.393, mean origin x 47.6. Non-win profile (25 matches): n_pass 256, reciprocity 0.394, mean out-degree 7.04, final-third share 0.079, long-pass share 0.381, mean origin x 46.4. Only n_pass (delta +41, 0/38 LOO flips, 89% bootstrap stability) and final-third share (delta +0.013, 0/38 LOO flips, 88% bootstrap, 6/7 opponent pairs) pass the action bar. Recommendations are stated as: keep the existing shape (it is stable and not the problem), train to the two robust levers, and monitor the two watch-list indicators.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What has been effective: (1) the midfield-driven, shape-stable passing structure itself — the M<->D corridor (3188 two-way passes over the season) and the 4x4 role web with full mutual linkage are present in wins and losses alike, so they are the reliable platform to build on, not a problem to fix; (2) high passing volume — wins average 297 passes versus 256 in non-wins, and the volume advantage is already present in the first half (R1), i.e. it is a tempo/possession strategy, not a lead-protection byproduct; (3) getting the ball into the opponent's final third — wins send 9.2% of passes there versus 7.9% in non-wins, and this is the only feature with a consistent sign across opponents (6/7 pairs). Recommended changes for next season, in priority order: (1) Tempo/rhythm as a training target — design training and in-game patterns that hold passing volume above the ~300-pass level in both halves; the data show the losses that hurt most are the low-volume ones (n_pass 109–247 in several losses), and volume is the single coefficient that survives every robustness check. (2) Final-third penetration as a measurable KPI — track per-game share of passes with destination x>80 and aim to raise the season mean from 0.080 toward the win-level 0.092; the role matrix shows the cleanest route is the M->F link (849 season passes) and the G->F launch (133 passes, mean distance 56.6), so the two highest-leverage drills are midfielder-to-forward service in the final third and goalkeeper launch accuracy into forwards. (3) Do not restructure the formation or the web — reciprocity and out-degree look large in the in-sample model but flip under refitting and have no consistent opponent signature; changing the shape risks losing the stable platform for no supported gain. Watch-list (monitor next season, do not act yet): reciprocity (it is higher in wins, 0.434 vs 0.394, and closed triads are over-represented in wins — 12.7% vs 8.9% of triads — but the coefficient is the least stable in R3/R4); mean origin x (wins play slightly deeper at origin, 47.6 vs 46.4 is actually reversed — wins' origins are marginally higher; the coefficient is negative and weak, so no action); long-pass share (no separation, 0.393 vs 0.381, and the coefficient is negative — the Huskies do NOT win by hitting more long balls; do not increase them). Caveats: the two levers were selected with the outcome in hand (post-hoc selection on the same 38 games), so the honest framing is that they are the only indicators that survived the pre-registered-style robustness battery, not that they are causally proven; confirming them requires a second season or held-out games, exactly the threshold the expert set. The advice is also limited to what the passing data can see — pressing, defending out of possession, set pieces and shot conversion are outside the supplied data and outside this model's scope.

tasks.task_description: Generalize the findings from this controlled team-sport setting to say something about how to design more effective teams in general, and identify what additional aspects of teamwork a generalized model of team performance would need to capture.
tasks.task_analysis: Generalization is done by mapping each soccer finding to its structural analogue in arbitrary teams, and by separating what the finding depends on about soccer (the rules that generate the data) from what it depends on about teams (the mechanisms that should transfer). The three findings that generalize are: (1) stable structure + variable execution — the web's shape was identical across wins and losses while the execution (where, how much risk) decided the matches, which is a general statement that a team's coordination structure is a slowly evolving asset and its match performance is driven by the fast variables a leader can set; (2) the missing-link bias — the network was built only from completed interactions, and the missing fraction was non-random (concentrated in the risky interactions), which is exactly how any interaction log in a team is biased toward safe, routine, successful interactions; (3) the role-vs-person identity problem — the data could not tell whether the same individual filled a role across games, which is a general identifiability constraint: without individual-level identity, only role-level statements are valid. The generalization claims are bounded: each is stated with the condition under which it would fail.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Mapping: soccer web shape -> any team's interaction graph (who communicates/depends on whom); pass volume -> throughput or interaction rate of the team; final-third share -> share of the team's output occurring in the high-value region of the task space; reciprocity -> balance of give-and-take in pairs; closed triads -> three-way coordination (no single point of failure in a 3-person subteam); missing failed passes -> unlogged failed interactions in any event data; slot labels -> role labels without individual IDs; the two-layer model (slow structure, fast execution) -> a general decomposition of team performance P into P = f(structure S, execution E, context C) where S changes on a season/quarter time scale, E on a task/game time scale, and C is the specific counterpart/task. The robustness protocol (game-state control, per-counterpart consistency, leave-one-out, bootstrap) generalizes as a template for any small-sample team-performance claim: control for the endogenous state (winning changes behaviour), check consistency across counterparts/tasks, and require sign stability under held-out refits before acting. No new parameters are introduced; the claim is structural, and its validity interval is 'teams whose interactions are logged event-by-event with role-level identifiers and a small number of repeated encounters' — outside that (e.g. no repeated encounters, or individual identity available), two of the three findings change form.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Generalized design principles, with their transfer conditions: (1) Separate the slow asset from the fast lever. In the Huskies data the coordination structure was stable across all 38 games and did not separate outcomes, while execution variables (interaction rate, output in the high-value region) did. For any team: invest in building a stable, well-connected coordination structure (the 'platform'), but manage performance through the fast variables — tempo, risk level, where effort is spent — because those are what vary between encounters and what a leader can actually set week to week. This transfers to any setting where the team's membership and roles are stable across many encounters and the encounters differ in conditions; it would fail for one-off projects where the structure is built per project. (2) Audit what your log does not contain. The passing network silently omitted every failed interaction, and the omission was concentrated exactly in the risky, forward, long interactions — so the network looked more connected and safer than the team actually was. Any team built on event logs (messages, tickets, commits, meetings) has the same bias: logs capture completed, usually successful, usually low-risk interactions. A generalized model must explicitly model the missing fraction and its correlation with risk/value, or it will overstate the team's connectivity and understate where it takes risks. This transfers universally to log-based team analysis. (3) Match the granularity of the identity to the claim. The data identified players only by role slot, so individual partnership claims were invalid and only role-level statements were supported. Generalized: a team model should state its identity granularity (individual, role, subteam) and restrict its claims to that level; claims about 'who works well with whom' require individual-level identity plus longitudinal tracking (substitution/subteam-change events), which the Huskies data lacked. (4) Small-sample discipline is part of the model, not an afterthought. With 38 encounters and 11 indicators, in-sample 'significant' numbers were common; only two indicators survived the robustness battery. Generalized models of team performance should treat sign stability under leave-one-out and bootstrap, control for endogenous state (performance changing behaviour), and consistency across counterpart tasks as part of the model's output, not optional post-hoc checks. What a fully generalized model would additionally need to capture, which this dataset could not: (a) individual identity over time (who fills which role, substitution/turnover dynamics) — needed to separate 'the team works well' from 'these individuals work well'; (b) the defensive/out-of-possession half of interaction — soccer is two-way, and the data only covered the Huskies' own ball possession, so the model saw only one team's behaviour in each match; a general model needs both sides' interaction streams; (c) the outcome-generating step between interaction and result — here, passes to shots to goals; in general, the causal path from team activity to the metric that matters, which requires event types beyond the interaction log (attempts, failures, external results); (d) time-resolved state — fatigue, momentum, score-state as a dynamic variable rather than a half split; (e) the counterfactual team — what the same individuals would do with different partners, which repeated-encounter data with turnover could support but this season's data does not; (f) multiple performance dimensions at once (wins, goals, quality, development) rather than a single win/loss label, since the three-class model's near-chance accuracy (0.474) shows the single label compresses too much information. Limitations of the generalization itself: it is drawn from one team, one season, one sport, one data source; the two robust levers (throughput, high-region output share) may be soccer-specific surface forms of more general variables, and confirming their generality requires teams from other domains with comparable event-level logs. The honest scope is: the structural template (slow structure / fast execution, missing-link audit, identity-granularity discipline, small-sample robustness battery) is the portable contribution; the specific indicator names are soccer-specific instantiations.
